items.title: Louis Keppard Interview, 1957-08-04
items.q: Well, Tickshaber was playing cornet, and this fellow, Lawrence Dewitt, was playing clarinet at that time with him.

ctx.x: Oakland right where Crozac is. Dates have their back entrance that Hall is given back there. Old man Umpra used to play with dear with Tick Chambers. You heard to talk about Tick Chambers? Yes, the Oakland Well, Tickshaber was playing cornet, and this fellow, Lawrence Dewitt, was playing clarinet at that time with him. And the old man, Umpra, was playing cyborg, clarinet over there with him also. Well, after he left, well, and the district closed down, well, they all reopened up with this fellow, little Willie…

You know, the rest of it. You know, it's just like, yeah, you see that voice note? Just like I said, well, I'm going to play in E-flat. All right, that voice note. Well, all the rest of the modern keys will follow right behind the system, brother. See? And every time they change, you can hear change, and in you lose. Is that going on here? Yes. Yes. I want to ask about this band, the one picture you have with Roy Palmer and Lawrence Dewey and Sugar Johnny. Yes, well, I'll tell you.

items.title: Lawrence Duhé Interview, 1957-06-09
items.q: Sugar Johnny, Louie Kepard on the guitar, Roy Palmer, Herbert Lindsay, Eddie Garland, and Toby Hall on the drums.

ctx.x: He had a big tone, most people say. Oh, it was a much more powerful man, but that style. That style, mm-hmm. When you went to Chicago, what was that date that tells here on this contract? That's April 1917. That's correct. Who all was in that band?
Sugar Johnny, Louie Kepard on the guitar, Roy Palmer, Herbert Lindsay, Eddie Garland, and Toby Hall on the drums.

items.title: Louis Keppard Interview, 1961-01-19
items.q: Well anyhow, then Lawrence Dewey, he got up there.

ctx.x: If you could tell us about some of the men on this picture.

You see now this here, this picture here, her husband is on this photograph, is her husband is the manager of the shore. Now she is black enough to impotate. She was a white person. She's a white person but she's black enough. This is nothing but a drop scenery but it's in Chicago, Illinois. That's during 1917. Now she's black enough to entertain. She's the dancer. Now her husband is the manager of the show. He's what they call a booking agent. That's her husband. And now the violin, he's leading the band. That's…
